[RESPONSE] I'm here for a follow-up about my Crohn disease, and I've also developed new-onset difficulty walking—people say I look like I'm "appearing drunk."

[THOUGHT] New-onset gait that makes others say you look "drunk" in a patient with Crohn disease raises strong possibilities: metronidazole-induced cerebellar toxicity (commonly used for Crohn perianal disease), vitamin deficiencies from ileal disease/resection (B12, vitamin E, copper), or other central causes. The quickest, highest-yield single question to distinguish a likely cause is recent metronidazole exposure because its neurotoxicity classically causes acute/subacute ataxia and is reversible after stopping; MRI can confirm. I will first ask about metronidazole use.

[QUERY] Have you taken metronidazole recently (in the past 3 months)? If yes, what dose and for how long?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall taking metronidazole in the past three months.

[THOUGHT] I need the time course to narrow causes: metronidazole toxicity and nutritional deficiencies have subacute onset over days–weeks; acute causes (stroke) are sudden. Knowing onset will direct next focused questions and tests. I'll ask one precise timing question.

[QUERY] When did the difficulty walking start — suddenly (over minutes–hours) or gradually (over days–weeks)? If gradual, how many days or weeks ago did it begin?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall whether the difficulty walking began suddenly or gradually, or how many days or weeks ago it started.

[THOUGHT] Medication history is critical to identify recent metronidazole or other neurotoxic drugs and supplements that could explain ataxia; this single focused question will guide next diagnostics.

[QUERY] Please list all current medications, recent antibiotics (including metronidazole) or supplements you’ve taken in the past 6 months, including doses if known.

[REFERENCE] 6. She has been on natalizumab for the past year.

[RESPONSE] I am currently on natalizumab and have been taking it for the past year. There is no other medication, recent antibiotic (including metronidazole), or supplement information provided here.

[THOUGHT] Natalizumab raises strong concern for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) presenting with subacute focal deficits, but cerebellar drug toxicity or nutritional causes remain possible. A focused neurologic symptom will help narrow causes (cerebellar lesions often cause dysarthria). I will ask one specific symptom question before ordering imaging.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any slurred speech or trouble forming words since the walking problems began?

[REFERENCE] 3. The patient reports new-onset difficulty walking, described by her peers as 'appearing drunk'.
11. Review_of_Systems: No additional symptoms provided.

[RESPONSE] No — I haven't noticed slurred speech or trouble forming words. Peers have said I appear "drunk" when walking, but I have no other symptoms to report.

[THOUGHT] A patient on natalizumab with new-onset "drunken" gait strongly raises concern for a central cerebellar or white-matter process — most urgently progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) from JC virus. MRI brain with appropriate sequences is the fastest, highest-yield test to detect cerebellar lesions, PML patterns, or stroke and will guide whether CSF JC PCR or other labs are needed. I will request an urgent brain MRI with contrast and diffusion sequences.

[TEST] Urgent MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast including FLAIR and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI).

8. MRI of the brain: Lesions consistent with Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML).
9. T1/T2 images showing multifocal demyelinating lesions without gadolinium enhancement, indicative of PML.
FLAIR: Normal
DWI: Normal

[THOUGHT] The MRI findings plus natalizumab therapy make PML the leading concern. The single most important confirmatory test is JC virus detection in CSF. I'll request a lumbar puncture specifically for JC virus PCR (with routine CSF studies as standard practice), which will confirm or refute PML and guide urgent management.

[TEST] Lumbar puncture: CSF JC virus PCR (and routine CSF studies: cell count, protein, glucose).

[THOUGHT] MRI plus natalizumab strongly suggest PML, but CSF JC virus PCR is required to confirm. The brief "Normal" CSF report is unclear about JC PCR status. I need the specific JC virus PCR result (and viral load if reported) because a negative PCR does not fully exclude PML and would change next steps (repeat LP, brain biopsy, or alternative diagnoses).

[QUERY] What was the CSF JC virus PCR result — positive or negative — and the reported viral load (copies/mL) if available?

[REFERENCE] N/A
[RESPONSE] I'm not sure — I don't recall the CSF JC virus PCR result or any reported viral load.

[THOUGHT] The MRI strongly suggests PML in a patient on natalizumab, but I still need the CSF JC virus PCR result (and viral load) to confirm the diagnosis and decide urgent management. I'll retrieve the specific CSF JC PCR result.

[TEST] Retrieve the CSF JC virus PCR result and reported viral load (copies/mL) from the lumbar puncture.

[THOUGHT] A patient on natalizumab with new-onset ataxic "drunken" gait and MRI showing multifocal, nonenhancing demyelinating lesions typical for PML makes JC virus–mediated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy the single most likely diagnosis. CSF studies may be falsely negative, but the clinical context and imaging are strongly supportive.

[DIAGNOSIS] Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus infection).
